meta.title: Who really said "On s'engage et puis... on voit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A chain of quotation, not an authorship. Lenin quoted it in 1923 and said 'Napoleon, I think, wrote…'. The maxim is in print by 1819 unattributed, credited in 1822 to the Russian general Kulnev, and only pinned on Napoleon decades after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'On s'engage et puis... on voit'?
meta.ogDescription: Lenin quoted it. Napoleon gets the credit. But the phrase is in print in 1819 with nobody's name on it, and an 1822 Prussian manual credits a Russian general instead.

answer.label: A military maxim of the Napoleonic era — author unproven
answer.authorDates: In print by 1819 · attached to Napoleon’s name only from the 1870s
answer.sourceLine: Two different questions get tangled here. Did Lenin quote it? Yes — in Our Revolution, written 16–17 January 1923, and he even hedged: ‘Napoleon, I think, wrote…’ Did Napoleon say it? No source has ever been produced. The maxim appears in print in a slightly longer form — on s’engage partout, et puis l’on voit — in 1819, in Napoleon’s own lifetime, with nobody’s name attached; an 1822 Prussian staff work credits it instead to the Russian general Yakov Kulnev. Napoleon’s name arrives later.

source.excerpt: On s'engage partout, et puis l'on voit.
trail: Start with the quoter. Lenin dictated Our Revolution (Apropos of N. Sukhanov’s Notes) on 16–17 January 1923; it ran in Pravda that May. The sentence is ‘Napoleon, I think, wrote: On s’engage et puis … on voit’ — and he glosses it as engaging in a serious battle first and seeing what follows the essay ↗.
That ‘I think’ is the tell. Lenin was passing on a maxim he had heard, not citing a text — and Wikiquote’s long, heavily sourced Napoleon page carries no entry for it at all.

Working backwards through digitised books, researchers on History Stack Exchange found the longer form on s’engage partout, et puis l’on voit in the Literarisches Wochenblatt in 1819 — unattributed — and in Georg Wilhelm von Valentini’s Die Lehre vom Krieg (1822), where it is credited to the Russian general Yakov Kulnev and tied to the Danube campaign of 1809–10 the archival dig ↗.

Napoleon’s name is attached from 1870 (Evelyn Baring’s Staff College Essays: ‘Napoleon’s motto was…’) and the short modern form is settled by 1889–1893, in a German military monthly, the French Revue d’artillerie and the US Journal of the Artillery. That is fifty to seventy years after his death — and thirty-odd years before Lenin picked it up. We have not inspected those volumes ourselves; we are reporting the Stack Exchange citations as found.
source.cutTag: The older, longer form — in print 1819
source.excerptNote: The form the maxim takes in the earliest printings, with partout — ‘one engages everywhere, and then one sees.’ The extra word is the useful one: it is what you search for if you want to find the phrase before Napoleon’s name got attached to it.
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. The maxim itself is anonymous and in print by 1819; the sources that carry it — Valentini 1822, Baring 1870, the military journals of 1889–93 — are all long out of copyright, as is Lenin’s 1923 essay. Only a specific modern English translation of Lenin would carry its own rights, and you do not need one for six words of French. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Napoleon
author.metaLine: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French, exiled to Elba in 1814
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte is the default owner of any crisp military maxim in French, which is exactly how a floating staff-college saying ends up with his name on it. The irony is that the sentiment cuts against his reputation: Napoleon is remembered as an obsessive planner, and this line is a shrug about not having a plan. It fits the man of 1796 far better than the man of 1812 — and no letter, dictation or memoir of his has ever been produced containing it.

misattribution.heading: Who said it and who merely quoted it
misattribution.intro: This is a chain of quotation rather than a straight misattribution, and each link is worth separating. One man made it famous, another gets the credit, and a third has the oldest claim on it.

items.who: Quoted it — did not coin it
items.why: Real, dated and verifiable: Our Revolution, 16–17 January 1923, published in Pravda that May. He used it to describe October 1917 — engage first, then find out what Brest-Litovsk and the New Economic Policy look like. He also wrote ‘I think,’ which is not how a man cites a text he has read read the passage ↗.

Nothing in the correspondence, the dictations or the memoirs of his companions. Wikiquote’s vast sourced Napoleon page has no entry for it. The earliest located instance, in 1819, is anonymous — printed while he was still alive on St Helena, and nobody thought to say it was his.

The Prussian officer G. W. von Valentini, in Die Lehre vom Krieg (1822), gives the saying to the Russian cavalry general Kulnev, associating it with the Danube fighting of 1809–10. Kulnev died in 1812. That is a named attribution eleven years before Napoleon’s death and half a century before anyone credits Napoleon.

The early form is on s’engage partout, et puis l’on voit — ‘one engages everywhere, and then one sees.’ The partout drops out over the century, leaving the tighter modern line. If you are hunting for a source, search the long form.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous maxim of the Napoleonic wars, in print by 1819 and credited in 1822 to a Russian general, not to Napoleon. Lenin quoted it in 1923 — and said ‘I think’ the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the most elegant defence of acting before you are ready ever compressed into six words, and it is beloved by exactly the people you would expect: generals, revolutionaries, founders and anyone about to do something they cannot fully justify in advance.

The pleasure of it is the pause. On s’engage et puis… — the ellipsis does the work, and then the flat, almost bored on voit. It sounds like someone who has already decided and is declining to argue about it.
detailsBody: 1809–10: the Danube campaign, where an 1822 Prussian source locates the Russian general Kulnev using the phrase.
1819: printed in the Literarisches Wochenblatt in the longer form, with no author named — Napoleon is still alive.
1822: Valentini’s Die Lehre vom Krieg credits it to Kulnev.
1870: Evelyn Baring’s Staff College Essays calls it ‘Napoleon’s motto’ — the earliest Napoleonic credit we have seen.
1889–1893: the short modern form circulates as Napoleon’s in German, French and American military journals.
January 1923: Lenin quotes it in Our Revolution and makes it famous outside the army.
context.pull: Lenin wrote 'Napoleon, I think, wrote…'. He was not sure either.
